extracted.intended_audience: aviation regulators, safety professionals, policymakers, industry analysts, and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Case analysis of Boeing 737 MAX design, certification, training, and organizational failures that contributed to two fatal accidents; identifies technical, regulatory, training, and governance shortcomings. Useful for assessing safety engineering and certification practices and for informing reform recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy is standard practice for critical components
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundancy is standard practice for critical components and systems in commercial aircraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AOA sensors can fail for many reasons; designs should build redundancy (multiple sensors) to avoid single points of failure. Example: 737 MAX had two AOA sensors but MCAS used data from only one; Airbus 320 and some Boeing aircraft use three sensors to provide double redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single point of failure in flight-control logic
rubrics_metrics.description: MCAS was designed to use data from only one of the sensors (alternating after each flight), creating a single point of failure hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flight-control logic should not depend on a single sensor reading — use cross-checking, majority-voting, or other redundancy-handling logic. Relying on a single sensor can permit erroneous inputs to trigger unsafe automated actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical alerts must be standard and operable
rubrics_metrics.description: The AOA indicator and disagree alert were not standard equipment on the 737 MAX; Boeing offered them as 'add ons' at additional cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety-critical cockpit alerts and indicators should be standard equipment and not tied to optional packages. Making them optional risks operators choosing cost savings over safety and can render critical warnings inoperable on many aircraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated systems should not hide failures from pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas MCAS was activated automatically, without pilot action, the cockpit crew would have to notice and act on an AOA DISAGREE alert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If systems act automatically (actuators moving without pilot input), their failure modes must be obvious and robustly communicated to crews; do not rely on optional displays or passive noticing. Automated actions should include fail-safes and clear, mandatory indications plus required pilot procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure of system changes to regulators during certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing included limited information in initial briefings to FAA on the MAX’s flight control software, MCAS, and presented the software as a modification to the existing speed trim system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers must fully disclose new or modified systems to certifying authorities and avoid framing significant changes as minor. Regulators need accurate, complete descriptions to scope appropriate review and testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report design changes and safety assessments in a timely manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing modified MCAS (increasing its authority and removing the G-force condition) during testing but did not submit certification documents to FAA detailing the change; formal safety risk assessments were not communicated until late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any design changes discovered during testing that alter system behavior or authority must be documented and reported promptly to certification authorities, accompanied by formal safety risk assessments so regulators can reassess risk and required mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess system-level safety risks at appropriate severity (e.g., catastrophic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing’s safety analysis did not assess system-level safety risks as catastrophic; thus MCAS was designed to rely on data from a single aircraft sensor rather than including redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate hazard severity classification is essential: if system-level failures could be catastrophic, design must include redundancies, fail-safes, and mitigations commensurate with that severity. Underestimating severity leads to inadequate designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot training must cover automated system activations and failure modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilot response to automated MCAS activation was not included in the required training; Boeing sought to avoid simulator training, advocating that CBT would be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training curricula should explicitly include automated system behaviors, failure modes, and recovery procedures. When aircraft handling or automation differs materially from prior models, hands-on simulator training should be required rather than only computer-based training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training level must be chosen based on actual aircraft differences (avoid minimal CBT when insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing proposed and obtained a 'Level B' training plan requiring only CBT for pilots already certified on prior 737s; pilot reaction to automated MCAS activation was not included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators and manufacturers should require training level (e.g., CBT vs. simulator) that reflects the scope and magnitude of differences; cost-saving aims should not drive under-training of crews for new system behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety-critical features should not be optional extras
rubrics_metrics.description: The disagree alert (and AOA indicator) was optional and not operable unless the airline purchased the optional AOA indicator; many carriers chose not to pay extra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features that materially affect safety should be required and provided as standard equipment. Allowing critical safety functionality to be optional creates inequitable safety baselines across operators and increases risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturers must transparently inform airlines when safety features are deactivated or changed
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing did not tell Southwest Airlines and other carriers when they began flying the 737 MAX jets that a safety feature found on earlier models that warns pilots about malfunctioning sensors had been deactivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators must be informed promptly and clearly about any removal, deactivation, or change to previously standard safety features so they can make informed purchase, configuration, and training decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure supplier parts are properly calibrated and maintenance records complete
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensor provided by a Florida-based company was not calibrated correctly nor did Lion Air maintenance crews detect the error when they installed the sensor; maintenance log pages were missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply-chain controls, part provenance, calibration procedures, and thorough maintenance logs are essential. Airlines and maintainers must verify calibration and complete maintenance documentation; manufacturers and suppliers must ensure quality of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate safety-related software across all marketed configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: A software bug meant that the warning light was working only if Lion Air purchased a package of equipment Boeing sold only as an option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software that supports safety functions must be validated for every configuration in which the aircraft will be sold or operated. Do not condition essential warnings on optional hardware or packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory independence, resourcing, and protection of specialist voices
rubrics_metrics.description: FAA safety personnel reported facing 'strong' external pressure from industry; many disagreed that the FAA 'makes data-driven decisions on safety regardless of external pressure.' Specialists felt overpowered in meetings with industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory agencies need sufficient resources, structural independence, and internal cultures that protect technical specialists from undue external or managerial pressure. Decision-making should be evidence-based and shielded from conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate governance structures should ensure safety independence and clear reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations included flipping reporting so senior engineers report 'primarily' to Boeing’s chief engineer, creation of a new safety group reporting to senior leadership and a permanent board committee focused on aerospace safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational reporting lines and governance should ensure safety organizations have independence, sufficient authority, and direct reporting paths to senior management and the board to prevent business pressures undermining safety decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing commercial incentives to compromise safety design and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing limited changes to 'avert a requirement that pilots spend time training in a flight simulator' and feared simulator training might limit sales; design/training choices were influenced by cost and sales concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business decisions (cost reduction, faster time-to-market, minimizing training burden) must not override safety-critical design and training requirements. Policies should guard against commercial pressures leading to unsafe compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulators must allocate review attention to all potentially risky changes, not only obvious high-risk areas
rubrics_metrics.description: FAA focused efforts on areas it identified as potentially high risk (larger engines, fly-by-wire spoilers, landing gear changes) and thus MCAS did not receive a more detailed review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification authorities should ensure their scoping and emphasis processes capture risks introduced by software, flight-control logic, and other less-visible changes. Relying solely on manufacturer characterizations of risk can miss critical system interactions.
